Lessons.Title: Solids of Rotation
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: A filled rectangle of width r revolved about its height-side sweeps a solid right circular cylinder of radius r; a right triangle revolved about a leg sweeps a cone. Naming an off-edge axis can create a hollow body.

Geometric reasoning: A filled rectangle of width r revolved about its height-side sweeps a solid right circular cylinder of radius r; a right triangle revolved about a leg sweeps a cone. Naming an off-edge axis can create a hollow body.

Verbal figure for this lesson: label the relevant centres, axes, dimensions and cutting planes before performing calculations; the construction/measurement constraints determine a unique valid model only when its hypotheses are satisfied.

Original source-specific task: Sketch and label two region/axis pairs and use a physical cutout or 3D visualizer to check the solid. Teacher reviews actual sketches and describes holes or interiors. Teacher rubric (0–4): labelled geometric hypotheses, correct transformation or dimensional formula, independent numerical checks and sound interpretation. Authentic diagrams and explanations must be teacher assessed, not assigned fictitious numeric grades.

Source alignment: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 1, CC BY 4.0. New Edulytiks examples independently authored; publisher graphics and protected assessments not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Axis of rotation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fixed line; points off axis trace circles whose radii are distances to the axis

KeyConcepts.Title: Filled generating region
KeyConcepts.Definition: Planar interior whose revolution sweeps 3D volume
KeyConcepts.Rule: Distinguish a region from merely its outline
KeyConcepts.Example: Rotating a rectangle gives a filled cylinder

KeyConcepts.Title: Generating profile
KeyConcepts.Definition: Perpendicular distances from axis describe cross-sectional radii
KeyConcepts.Rule: A linear taper makes a cone
KeyConcepts.Example: Right triangle gives cone or double cone depending on axis

WorkedExamples.Title: Solids of Rotation: investigation 1
WorkedExamples.Question: A filled rectangle 3 wide and 7 high rotates about its 7-unit side. Identify solid and dimensions.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use axis of rotation with explicit geometric hypotheses.
Steps: The side of length 7 is the fixed axis
Every height level sweeps a disk of radius 3
The union of disks forms cylinder of height 7
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify units, nondegeneracy and the stated relationship independently.

WorkedExamples.Title: Solids of Rotation: investigation 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Right triangle has legs 4 and 6. Rotate about the 6-leg.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use filled generating region with explicit geometric hypotheses.
Steps: Six-unit leg is the stationary axis
The four-unit leg traces a disk radius 4 at one end
Radial extent tapers linearly to apex
WorkedExamples.Answer: Right circular cone of radius 4 and height 6.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify units, nondegeneracy and the stated relationship independently.

WorkedExamples.Title: Solids of Rotation: investigation 3
WorkedExamples.Question: A filled semicircle radius 5 rotates around its diameter.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use generating profile with explicit geometric hypotheses.
Steps: The diameter is the axis through the circle centre
Circular slices sweep all radial directions
The entire 3D ball of radius 5 is swept
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify units, nondegeneracy and the stated relationship independently.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mistaking an outline for the filled region
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An outline sweeps surfaces, not necessarily the filled interior
Changing axes can change solid shape and dimensions

SummaryPoints: A filled rectangle of width r revolved about its height-side sweeps a solid right circular cylinder of radius r; a right triangle revolved about a leg sweeps a cone. Naming an off-edge axis can create a hollow body.
Distinguish a region from merely its outline
The drawn model and justified explanation require authentic teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Slicing Solids
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: A plane cross section is the full intersection with a solid. Planes parallel to a right cylinder's bases give disks; a plane through its axis yields a rectangle; a pyramid's parallel slices are smaller similar polygons.

Geometric reasoning: A plane cross section is the full intersection with a solid. Planes parallel to a right cylinder's bases give disks; a plane through its axis yields a rectangle; a pyramid's parallel slices are smaller similar polygons.

Verbal figure for this lesson: label the relevant centres, axes, dimensions and cutting planes before performing calculations; the construction/measurement constraints determine a unique valid model only when its hypotheses are satisfied.

Original source-specific task: Draw three differently oriented planes through an original cylinder model and explain resulting cuts. Teacher scores the diagrams and argument. Teacher rubric (0–4): labelled geometric hypotheses, correct transformation or dimensional formula, independent numerical checks and sound interpretation. Authentic diagrams and explanations must be teacher assessed, not assigned fictitious numeric grades.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cross section
KeyConcepts.Definition: Intersection of solid and plane including interior
KeyConcepts.Example: Horizontal slice of vertical cylinder is a disk

KeyConcepts.Title: Parallel prism sections
KeyConcepts.Definition: For a uniform prism, base-parallel sections are congruent

KeyConcepts.Title: Pyramid sections
KeyConcepts.Definition: Planes parallel to base produce similar scaled base figures
KeyConcepts.Rule: Linear size changes with distance from apex
KeyConcepts.Example: Halfway from apex gives quarter area

WorkedExamples.Title: Slicing Solids: investigation 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Cylinder radius 3 and height 8 sliced parallel to base at height 5. Describe section.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use cross section with explicit geometric hypotheses.
Steps: Cut is perpendicular to vertical axis
At height 5 all points within radius 3 are included
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify units, nondegeneracy and the stated relationship independently.

WorkedExamples.Title: Slicing Solids: investigation 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Square pyramid base side 6 sliced halfway from apex parallel to base.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use parallel prism sections with explicit geometric hypotheses.
Steps: All rays from apex are intercepted at half-distance
Section side is half of 6, namely 3
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify units, nondegeneracy and the stated relationship independently.

WorkedExamples.Title: Slicing Solids: investigation 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Rectangular prism 2 by 3 by 7 sliced parallel to its 2-by-3 face.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use pyramid sections with explicit geometric hypotheses.
Steps: Cross section duplicates the chosen face
Side lengths are 2 and 3 at any interior depth
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify units, nondegeneracy and the stated relationship independently.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Axial cuts can be rectangles and oblique cuts ellipses
The cut is the entire plane-solid intersection
CommonMistakes.Correction: Draw the interior of the intersection

SummaryPoints: A plane cross section is the full intersection with a solid. Planes parallel to a right cylinder's bases give disks; a plane through its axis yields a rectangle; a pyramid's parallel slices are smaller similar polygons.
The drawn model and justified explanation require authentic teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Creating Cross Sections by Dilating
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: A plane section of a pyramid or cone parallel to its base is the dilation image of the base with centre at apex. At fraction t of apex-to-base height, corresponding lengths scale by t and areas by t².

Geometric reasoning: A plane section of a pyramid or cone parallel to its base is the dilation image of the base with centre at apex. At fraction t of apex-to-base height, corresponding lengths scale by t and areas by t².

Verbal figure for this lesson: label the relevant centres, axes, dimensions and cutting planes before performing calculations; the construction/measurement constraints determine a unique valid model only when its hypotheses are satisfied.

Original source-specific task: Draw elevation and three apex-parallel slices; label centres and verify their area ratios. Teacher assesses original drawing. Teacher rubric (0–4): labelled geometric hypotheses, correct transformation or dimensional formula, independent numerical checks and sound interpretation. Authentic diagrams and explanations must be teacher assessed, not assigned fictitious numeric grades.

Source alignment: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 3, CC BY 4.0. New Edulytiks examples independently authored; publisher graphics and protected assessments not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Apex-centred dilation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Maps base to a parallel plane section of a pyramid
KeyConcepts.Rule: Scale by distance from apex divided by full height
KeyConcepts.Example: At t=1/3 a 12-unit edge maps to 4

KeyConcepts.Title: Section area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area is quadratic in linear scale

KeyConcepts.Title: Height reference
KeyConcepts.Definition: Distance must be measured from apex for this t
KeyConcepts.Rule: Convert height above base to apex distance
KeyConcepts.Example: Height 2 above base in height 8 gives t=6/8

WorkedExamples.Title: Creating Cross Sections by Dilating: investigation 1
WorkedExamples.Question: Square pyramid height 12 base side 10. Slice 3 below apex.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use apex-centred dilation with explicit geometric hypotheses.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify units, nondegeneracy and the stated relationship independently.

WorkedExamples.Title: Creating Cross Sections by Dilating: investigation 2
WorkedExamples.Question: Cone radius 8 height 15. Find radius at section 6 from apex.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use section area with explicit geometric hypotheses.
Steps: The parallel plane cuts a similar circle
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify units, nondegeneracy and the stated relationship independently.

WorkedExamples.Title: Creating Cross Sections by Dilating: investigation 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Pyramid base area 144 sliced halfway between apex and base.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use height reference with explicit geometric hypotheses.
WorkedExamples.Check: Verify units, nondegeneracy and the stated relationship independently.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The dilation is centred at apex

SummaryPoints: A plane section of a pyramid or cone parallel to its base is the dilation image of the base with centre at apex. At fraction t of apex-to-base height, corresponding lengths scale by t and areas by t².
The drawn model and justified explanation require authentic teacher review.

Lessons.Title: Scaling and Unscaling
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: For positive areas, image/source area ratio q=k² and the positive linear scale k=√q. Graph y=k² on k≥0 and its inverse y=√q; reciprocal scale reverses the dilation.
Geometric reasoning: For positive areas, image/source area ratio q=k² and the positive linear scale k=√q. Graph y=k² on k≥0 and its inverse y=√q; reciprocal scale reverses the dilation.
